subject: Agriculture
title: School Feeding Programs
description: A micro-lesson that makes School Feeding Programs usable.

hook.text: School meals are the world's largest social safety net—388 million children receive them daily.

buildup.text: For many children in developing countries, the school meal is the only reliable meal of the day.

discovery.text: School feeding increases enrollment, especially for girls. Families send children to school when food is guaranteed.

twist.text: During COVID school closures, 370 million children suddenly lost their main meal source. Hunger surged.

climax.text: Linking school meals to local farmers creates markets for smallholders while feeding children—a double win.

punchline.text: Feed a child at school and you fund both education and nutrition.

quiz.question: How many children worldwide receive school meals daily?

details.summary: School feeding programs provide meals or snacks to children in educational settings. This topic covers how these programs improve nutrition, boost school attendance, and can create local food markets that benefit smallholder farmers in poor communities.
details.whyItMatters: For 73 million children in extreme poverty, a school meal may be the only reliable nutrition they receive. These programs simultaneously fight hunger, improve learning, and keep kids in school.
takeaways: Around 388 million children receive school meals in 161 countries worldwide
School feeding increases enrollment and attendance by 8–12% in low-income areas
Home-grown school feeding links programs to local farmers, boosting rural economies

faq.question: How do school feeding programs affect educational outcomes?
faq.answer: School meals boost enrollment, reduce absenteeism, improve concentration and test scores, and decrease dropout rates. Well-nourished children learn more effectively, and the promise of a meal gives families strong incentive to send children to school.

faq.question: What is home-grown school feeding?
faq.answer: Home-grown school feeding sources meals from local smallholder farmers rather than imported commodities. This creates a reliable market for local producers, keeps money in rural economies, and provides children with fresh, culturally appropriate foods.
